blocks.text: The core respiratory symptoms are **cough, sputum, haemoptysis, breathlessness, wheeze and chest pain**. Also ask about fever, night sweats, weight loss, malaise and hoarseness. For each symptom, establish how fast it started, how it has changed since, and whether it varies with time or place.

blocks.title: Cough: what the pattern suggests
rows: Upper or lower respiratory tract infection, inhaled irritant
Upper airway cough syndrome (post-nasal drip), asthma, GORD, COPD, bronchiectasis, ACE inhibitor, lung cancer, heart failure
COPD / chronic bronchitis (smokers often cough in the morning with little sputum)
Asthma (cough may be its only feature) or acid reflux
Copious sputum, provoked by changes of posture
Worse lying flat, pink frothy secretions
Dry and tickly on an ACE inhibitor
Drug cough: 10–15% of users, more often women
A cough that is getting worse in a smoker
Lung cancer (its most frequent presenting symptom)

blocks.title: The sound of the cough
items: **Bovine cough:** hollow, low-pitched and without the normal explosive start, with hoarseness. A vocal cord cannot close, e.g. left recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy from a lung tumour.
**Loud brassy cough:** a tumour compressing the trachea.
**Barking cough:** croup or tracheomalacia.
In adults, **pertussis** can cause a cough lasting up to 3 months.

blocks.text: Chronic cough with a **normal examination, chest X-ray and spirometry** is usually **cough-variant asthma, post-nasal drip or GORD**, so check for an ACE inhibitor first.

blocks.title: Sputum appearance
rows: Clear or white (mucoid), sometimes black carbon specks
Bronchial or pneumonic infection, but the colour comes from cells (neutrophils or eosinophils), so it can also occur in asthma

blocks.title: Haemoptysis: first confirm it is real
items: **Haemoptysis:** blood is coughed up and mixed with sputum.
**Haematemesis:** blood follows nausea or retching and is mixed with vomit.
**Nose, gum or nasopharyngeal bleeding:** blood simply appears in the mouth without a cough.
Once it is confirmed, **assume a serious cause** until investigations exclude one.

blocks.title: Haemoptysis: history clue and likely cause
rows: Repeated small bleeds or blood streaks, smoker, hoarseness
Fever, night sweats, weight loss, TB contact or HIV
Large volumes of sputum with blood, often a past history of TB or childhood pneumonia
Acute fever and dyspnoea, rusty sputum
Pleuritic pain and breathlessness, leg swelling
Orthopnoea, pink froth, or a mitral murmur

blocks.text: In Talley, **bronchitis, bronchial carcinoma, bronchiectasis and pneumonia** account for about 80% of haemoptysis. Davidson lists cancer, bronchiectasis, acute bronchitis, TB, pulmonary infarction and acute LVF as its commoner causes. Many episodes stay unexplained after full investigation and are probably simple bronchial infection.

blocks.title: Managing haemoptysis
items: **Severe bleeding:** sit the patient upright, or lie them on the bleeding side if that is known. Give high-flow oxygen and resuscitate.
Tranexamic acid or terlipressin may reduce bleeding, but the evidence is limited. **Bronchial artery embolisation** or emergency surgery can save life.
**Usual (non-massive) case:** chest X-ray, FBC and clotting screen, **bronchoscopy once bleeding settles**, and CTPA (PE, AVM, hidden tumour).

blocks.text: **Massive haemoptysis cut-offs differ between books:** Talley says over 250 mL in 24 h and Kumar says over 200 mL in 24 h. Davidson gives no figure on these pages. Either way it is an emergency, usually from cancer, bronchiectasis, TB or CF. Mild haemoptysis is under about 20 mL a day, seen as streaks.
A **normal chest X-ray does not rule out** a serious cause of haemoptysis. However, when the X-ray is normal, CT and bronchoscopy find a diagnosis in only about 5%.

sections.title: Breathlessness, wheeze, chest pain and other symptoms

blocks.text: Dyspnoea is an uncomfortable awareness of needing to breathe that feels out of proportion to the activity. Lung disease drives it in three ways: **stimulating intrapulmonary sensory nerves** (pneumothorax, PE, interstitial inflammation), **increasing the mechanical load** on the breathing muscles (airflow obstruction, fibrosis), and **hypoxia, hypercapnia or acidosis** acting on chemoreceptors. Make sure chest tightness is not actually angina.

blocks.title: Breathlessness by speed of onset
rows: Asthma, PE, pneumothorax (instant), pulmonary oedema, anaphylaxis, inhaled foreign body, arrhythmia, MI
Pneumonia, COPD exacerbation, heart failure, metabolic acidosis
COPD, ILD / fibrosis, pleural effusion, malignancy, anaemia, heart failure, neuromuscular disease

blocks.title: Questions that sort chronic breathlessness
items: **At rest and overnight?** COPD limits mainly walking, with few symptoms at rest. Asthma often wakes the patient with tightness and wheeze.
**Does it vary?** Variation from day to day or hour to hour is the hallmark of asthma. A slow, steady decline over months to years fits COPD.
**Relentless, present even at rest, with a dry cough?** Think interstitial fibrosis.
**Childhood wheeze, eczema, hay fever, family atopy?** These make asthma more likely.
**Morning headache?** It may mean CO2 retention, especially in kyphoscoliosis or muscle disease.
**Angina, MI, hypertension?** These favour a cardiac cause.

blocks.title: Grading breathlessness
rows: No dyspnoea, or only on heavy exertion
When hurrying or walking up a slight hill
Walks slower than peers on the level, or stops at own pace
Stops after about 100 m on the level
Housebound by breathlessness, or breathless when dressing

blocks.text: Writing "breathless on exertion" is not enough. Record **how far the patient walks on the level and how many stairs or inclines** they manage on a good day.

**Orthopnoea is not specific to heart failure.** Kumar says it is classically linked to heart failure, although the abdominal contents pushing the diaphragm up also contribute, and Talley lists PND as a clue to cardiac failure. Davidson (primary) notes that lying flat pushes the diaphragm up and worsens airflow obstruction, so orthopnoea is common in COPD. It only points to the heart when there is a cardiac history. PND remains typical of left heart failure.

**Psychogenic hyperventilation:** the patient cannot get a satisfying deep breath and sighs often. It comes with perioral or finger tingling and occurs at rest, rarely at night. Nijmegen score over 26, resting end-tidal CO2 under 4.5%. ABG: **normal PO2, low PCO2, alkalosis**. Diagnose it only after excluding other causes, especially thromboembolism.

**Wheeze** is a continuous whistling sound, loudest on expiration. **Stridor** is a harsh noise on _inspiration_, loudest over the trachea, from narrowing of a major (upper) airway. It needs urgent assessment. Sudden causes include anaphylaxis, epiglottitis, foreign body and toxic gas. Gradual causes include laryngeal or tracheal tumour, bilateral cord palsy and nodal compression.

**Wheeze does not mean asthma.** It reflects airflow limitation from any cause, e.g. COPD, bronchiolitis or vocal cord dysfunction, and it can be absent in early asthma. Wheeze heard on one side only suggests a focal lesion.

blocks.title: Chest pain in respiratory patients
rows: Sharp, localised, worse on deep breath or cough (pleuritic)
Parietal pleura involved. When sudden with dyspnoea: pneumonia, PE/infarction, pneumothorax
Malignant invasion of the chest wall

blocks.title: Other symptoms to ask about
items: **Obstructive sleep apnoea:** airflow stops for 10 s or longer despite breathing effort. It causes daytime sleepiness, fatigue, morning headache and loud snoring. Witnessed choking or gasping is more reliable than snoring (LR 3.3). Epworth score: 0–9 is normal.
**Hoarseness:** laryngitis, vocal cord tumour, or recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy.
**Night sweats, weight loss, malaise:** TB or malignancy.
**Upper airway:** thin watery discharge suggests allergic rhinitis. Blood-stained discharge with obstruction and pain may mean a nasal tumour. Polyps block the nose and dull smell.

sections.title: Drug, occupational, social and family history

blocks.title: Drugs to ask about
rows: Beta-blockers (including timolol eye drops), aspirin and NSAIDs

blocks.title: Treatment and past history
items: **Oral steroids** predispose to TB and pneumocystis pneumonia.
**Using more reliever (bronchodilator)** means asthma is poorly controlled.

**Home oxygen:** usually 2 L/min or more. It needs a blood gas showing low oxygen and requires that the patient has stopped smoking. Also ask about pulmonary rehabilitation and airway-clearance physiotherapy.
**Past history:** pneumonia, TB, abnormal chest X-rays, bronchoscopy, and past spirometry or peak flow results.
**Childhood:** prematurity, whooping cough, measles.
People with **AIDS** are at high risk of _Pneumocystis jirovecii_ pneumonia and TB.

blocks.text: The occupational history matters more in respiratory medicine than in any other system. Ask about **every job ever held** and whether symptoms relate to work. The **commonest occupational lung disease is asthma**, and feeling better at weekends or on holiday is the key clue. The pneumoconioses (coal, silica, asbestos, talc) cause interstitial disease after long exposure. Also ask about organic dusts (hay, mushrooms, cotton), animals and travel (TB risk).

blocks.title: Asbestos
items: **Heavy exposure** causes asbestosis. **Even trivial exposure** can cause mesothelioma.
Disease can appear **up to 30 years** after exposure.
At-risk groups include dockyard workers, builders, demolition and renovation workers, and **relatives who washed work clothes**.

blocks.title: Extrinsic allergic alveolitis (hypersensitivity pneumonitis)
rows: A flu-like illness a few hours after exposure: fever, myalgia, dry cough and breathlessness, **without wheeze**

blocks.title: Social and family history
items: **Smoking:** calculate pack-years and record quit attempts and use of nicotine replacement or e-cigarettes. Smoking causes COPD and lung cancer and raises the risk of ILD, pneumothorax and Goodpasture disease. Ask about passive smoking and smoked cannabis.
**Alcohol binges** lead to aspiration and pneumococcal or _Klebsiella_ pneumonia. **IV drug use** leads to lung abscess. Ask about HIV risk.
**Family history:** asthma and atopy, cystic fibrosis, alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency (inherited emphysema), bronchiectasis, lung cancer, TB contacts, pulmonary hypertension.

blocks.text: Features that point to **asthma**: episodic symptoms, worse at night or early morning, dry cough with wheeze and breathlessness, personal or family atopy. Triggers include infection, exercise, animals, cold, damp or dusty air, and emotion.

**Exam keyword pairs:** smoker + haemoptysis + clubbing means bronchial carcinoma. Haemoptysis + weight loss + night sweats means TB. A tall, thin young smoker with sudden pain and dyspnoea has a primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Wheeze about an hour after aspirin means aspirin-sensitive asthma. Immobility or the pill with acute dyspnoea means PE.
**COPD does not cause clubbing** and rarely causes haemoptysis or chest pain. If any of these appears in a COPD patient, look for something else, especially lung cancer.

sections.title: General inspection, hands, face and neck

blocks.title: Setting up and looking around
items: Undress the patient to the waist (offer women a gown) and sit them on the edge of the bed.
Look around the bed for oxygen (mask or nasal prongs), inhalers, nebulisers and the **sputum pot**, and check the observation chart for SpO2 and inspired oxygen.
From the end of the bed, note alertness, posture, cachexia, fever, breathlessness at rest and any rash.

blocks.text: **Respiratory rate:** normal is up to about 25/min (range 16–25, average 20). **Tachypnoea** is over 25/min. **Bradypnoea** is under 8/min and goes with sedation and a poor prognosis. Count it discreetly while you appear to take the pulse, because breathing is under voluntary control.

blocks.title: Increased work of breathing (e.g. severe COPD)
items: Accessory muscle use: sternocleidomastoid, platysma and strap muscles, lifting the shoulders on inspiration
Pursed-lip breathing; sitting forward with arms braced on the knees
Intercostal and supraclavicular in-drawing on inspiration; tracheal tug

blocks.title: Abnormal breathing patterns
rows: Cheyne–Stokes: apnoea alternating with deepening then fading breaths
Left ventricular failure, brain damage, high altitude

blocks.title: Cyanosis
items: **Central cyanosis:** look at the tongue (especially underneath) and lips. It appears at about **50 g/L of deoxygenated haemoglobin**, usually when SaO2 is below 90% with a normal Hb.
It appears **later in anaemia**, and its absence does not exclude hypoxia.
Central cyanosis is always accompanied by peripheral cyanosis. **Isolated peripheral cyanosis** (cold hands, blue nails) means poor peripheral circulation.

blocks.title: Hand signs
rows: Lung cancer, suppurative lung disease, fibrosis, mesothelioma (see below)
Smoking. Its density reflects how the cigarette is held, not how many are smoked
Wasting of small hand muscles, weak finger abduction
Warm palms, bounding pulse, coarse flap
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (lung cancer, pleural fibroma)
Yellow nail syndrome (pleural effusion, bronchiectasis, lymphoedema)

blocks.text: **Finger clubbing** is painless soft-tissue swelling of the fingertip. The angle between the nail and the nail fold (hyponychial angle) is lost, the nail curves more in every direction, and the nail bed feels fluctuant. Lifting of the proximal nail makes the finger thicker front-to-back at the nail base than at the DIP joint. Over 90% of cases mean serious disease.

blocks.title: Causes of clubbing
rows: Suppuration (bronchiectasis, CF, lung abscess, empyema, TB); tumours (lung cancer, mesothelioma, fibroma); pulmonary fibrosis
Cyanotic congenital heart disease, infective endocarditis, arteriovenous shunts, atrial myxoma
Cirrhosis, inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease

blocks.text: A classic "clubbing **except**" item: **uncomplicated COPD (chronic bronchitis/emphysema) does not cause clubbing**. New clubbing in a COPD patient needs another explanation.
The **CO2 retention flap** (cycle of 2–3 s) is a late and unreliable sign and also occurs in liver and renal failure. Look for warm hands, a bounding pulse and confusion as well.

blocks.title: Face and neck
items: **Horner syndrome** (small pupil, partial ptosis, loss of sweating) from an apical Pancoast tumour.
**SVC obstruction:** facial plethora and swelling, dilated neck and chest-wall veins. In a positive **Pemberton sign**, raising the arms causes facial congestion.
Nasal polyps (asthma); poor teeth (lung abscess); crowded pharynx (sleep apnoea); anaemia; pursed lips.
**Lymph nodes:** cervical, supraclavicular and axillary. In lung cancer the supraclavicular nodes are often the first enlarged nodes found.
**Raised JVP** with ankle or sacral oedema suggests cor pulmonale.

blocks.note: Look at: front and side views of clubbed fingers. Note the loss of the nail-fold angle and the bulbous fingertip.
Look at: thick yellow nails with onycholysis (yellow nail syndrome), linked to effusions, bronchiectasis and lymphoedema.

sections.title: Chest: inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation

blocks.title: Inspecting the chest
items: **Barrel chest:** an AP-to-lateral diameter ratio over 0.9 suggests hyperinflation (emphysema, severe asthma), but it can be normal in old age.
**Pectus excavatum** (funnel chest), **pectus carinatum** (pigeon chest, after childhood lung disease or rickets), Harrison sulcus, and **kyphoscoliosis** (asymmetry).

**Scars:** a long posterior thoracotomy scar (lobectomy or pneumonectomy) or small VATS ports. Also look for radiotherapy marks and tattoos, subcutaneous emphysema (usually pneumothorax) and dilated veins (SVC obstruction).
**Movement:** reduced movement on one side means a lesion on that side (consolidation, collapse, effusion, pneumothorax, localised fibrosis). Reduction on both sides suggests COPD or diffuse ILD.

blocks.title: Tracheal position
rows: Upper lobe collapse, upper lobe fibrosis, pneumonectomy
Retrosternal goitre. Slight deviation to the right can be normal

blocks.title: Palpation
items: Check the trachea and apex beat; an impalpable apex suggests hyperinflation.
**Cricosternal distance** (cricoid to sternal notch) is normally 3–4 finger-breadths in full expiration and is **reduced in severe airflow limitation**.

**Expansion:** on a deep breath the thumbs should separate symmetrically by **at least 5 cm**. Assess the upper lobes by watching the clavicles from behind. Use a tape measure for serial readings, e.g. in ankylosing spondylitis.
**Hoover sign:** in a hyperinflated COPD chest the costal margins move **inward** on inspiration (LR+ 4.2).
**Tactile vocal fremitus** duplicates vocal resonance and is damped or abolished by pleural fluid.
Costochondral tenderness suggests costochondritis. Pain on compressing the chest suggests a rib fracture.

blocks.title: Percussion note
rows: Normally 6th intercostal space, right midclavicular line. Lower, or lost along with cardiac dullness, means hyperinflation

blocks.title: Breath sounds
rows: Rustling; inspiration louder and longer than expiration with no gap
Healthy lung, which filters out the high frequencies
Hollow, blowing; gap between phases; expiration as long or louder and higher-pitched
Consolidation (needs patent airways), localised fibrosis, collapse with an open bronchus, just above an effusion
Effusion, pneumothorax, collapse with blocked bronchus, severe obstruction

blocks.title: Added sounds
rows: Widespread narrowing of many small airways (asthma, COPD)
Fixed monophonic wheeze that does not clear on coughing
A single partly blocked bronchus, e.g. bronchial carcinoma
Coarse gurgling crackles that change after a cough
Pleural rub: localised creak, like footsteps in fresh snow
Pleurisy, e.g. pneumonia or pulmonary infarction

blocks.title: Vocal resonance
items: **Increased** over consolidation: the spoken voice sounds louder and bleating (**aegophony**, "ee" heard as "ay"), and whispers are clearly heard (**whispering pectoriloquy**).
**Reduced or absent** over an effusion, pneumothorax or blocked bronchus.

blocks.text: **A silent chest is not reassuring.** In life-threatening asthma, airflow may be too low to produce a wheeze. Wheeze loudness is a poor guide to severity.

**Crackles in consolidation:** Kumar's signs table (Box 28.8) lists _fine_ crackles, but Kumar's own examination diagram and Zero to Finals describe _coarse_ crackles in pneumonia. Davidson (primary) does not name a type, and Talley grades crackles by timing. For exams, rely on dullness, bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance.

blocks.title: Completing the examination
items: Heart: JVP at 45°, and a loud or palpable P2 (pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale).
Abdomen: a liver pushed down by hyperinflation, or metastases.
Pemberton sign (SVC obstruction), leg oedema and signs of DVT, temperature.
Inspect the sputum pot and measure peak flow or spirometry.

blocks.note: Look at: increased AP diameter of a barrel-shaped, hyperinflated chest.
Look at: funnel chest (pectus excavatum) compared with pigeon chest (pectus carinatum).
Look at: Hoover sign, where the costal margins move inward on inspiration in a hyperinflated chest.

sections.title: Putting the signs together and bedside tests

blocks.title: Signs of common lung lesions
rows: Reduced or absent; bronchial above the fluid
Fine late inspiratory crackles; often clubbed
Resonant; cardiac and liver dullness lost

blocks.text: **Diffuse fibrosis percussion:** Kumar's table gives a normal note, but Davidson (primary) describes **dullness at the bases** from small lungs with a high diaphragm. Go with Davidson.

**Tension pneumothorax** is an emergency: a one-way valve keeps trapping air. The patient is tachypnoeic, cyanosed, tachycardic and may be hypotensive. The trachea and apex are pushed to the other side; the affected side is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds and vocal resonance. Decompress immediately without waiting for an X-ray. The Zero to Finals exam answer is a large-bore cannula in the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line. Davidson adds that releasing the pressure with a cannula buys time to insert a chest drain.

**Right upper lobe collapse** (Davidson): trachea pulled to the right, reduced volume and expansion in the right upper zone, dull note, reduced breath sounds if a central bronchus is blocked. CXR shows an **elevated horizontal fissure** and possibly a hilar mass.

blocks.title: How much do signs help? (likelihood ratios)
rows: Smoking history + forced expiratory time ≥9 s
Two or more of: >40 pack-years, prior COPD diagnosis, reduced breath sounds

blocks.title: Signs of respiratory distress or failure
items: Cyanosis or low SpO2; accessory muscle use; unable to speak in sentences
Very fast or very slow breathing; exhaustion; drowsiness (pre-terminal)
Silent chest; stridor; tachycardia; pulsus paradoxus

blocks.title: Acute asthma severity
rows: PEF 33–50% of predicted, RR >25, HR >110, cannot finish sentences
PEF <33%, SpO2 <92%, silent chest, exhaustion, haemodynamic instability
Cyanosis, drowsiness, pulse >130/min and pulsus paradoxus >20 mmHg mark severe asthma

blocks.title: Bedside lung function
items: **Forced expiratory time:** 3 s or less is normal. With a smoking history, 9 s or more strongly suggests COPD.
**Peak flow:** about 600 L/min in young men and 400 L/min in young women. It is effort-dependent and most useful as serial readings (asthma variability).
**Spirometry, obstructive:** FEV1/FVC <70% with a disproportionately low FEV1 (asthma, COPD). Reversibility after a bronchodilator favours asthma.
**Spirometry, restrictive:** FEV1 and FVC both reduced with a normal or high ratio (ILD, sarcoidosis, chest wall disease).
Peak flow or spirometry measures airflow limitation better than any physical sign.

blocks.note: Look at: spirometry traces. Normal has FEV1/FVC about 80%, obstructive about 42%, restrictive about 90% with small volumes.
Look at: left upper lobe collapse, with hazy left upper and mid zones and the trachea and heart pulled to the left.

cards.back: Over 250 mL in 24 h (Talley) or over 200 mL in 24 h (Kumar). It is an emergency either way. Mild is under about 20 mL a day.

cards.front: What proportion of ACE inhibitor users develop a dry chronic cough?

cards.back: A vocal cord cannot close, e.g. recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (often from lung cancer). The cough loses its explosive start.
Stops for breath after about 100 m on the level.
Normal PO2, low PCO2 and alkalosis. Exclude thromboembolism before making the diagnosis.

cards.front: Stridor vs wheeze: timing and site?
cards.back: Stridor is inspiratory and loudest over the trachea (upper airway obstruction). Wheeze is mainly expiratory (intrathoracic airways).

cards.front: Four drugs that cause interstitial lung disease?
Farmer's lung: what is the exposure?
cards.back: Mouldy hay or straw (_Aspergillus fumigatus_). Flu-like symptoms come a few hours after exposure, without wheeze.

cards.front: Commonest occupational lung disease and its key clue?
cards.back: Asthma. Symptoms improve at weekends or on holiday.

cards.front: Central cyanosis appears at about what level of deoxygenated Hb?
cards.back: About 50 g/L of capillary blood (SaO2 usually <90%). It appears later in anaemia.
No. New clubbing in a COPD patient means looking for another cause, especially lung cancer.

cards.front: Pancoast tumour: hand and eye signs?
cards.back: Wasting of the small hand muscles (T1 invasion) and Horner syndrome (miosis, partial ptosis, anhidrosis).

cards.front: Causes that pull the trachea towards the lesion?
cards.back: Upper lobe collapse, upper lobe fibrosis, pneumonectomy. Massive effusion and tension pneumothorax push it away.
Pulmonary fibrosis / ILD. Early inspiratory crackles suggest small airways disease (COPD).

cards.front: Signs of a large pleural effusion?
cards.back: Reduced expansion, stony dull note, absent breath sounds and vocal resonance, sometimes bronchial breathing above. The trachea shifts away only if the effusion is massive.

cards.front: Normal forced expiratory time, and the spirometry cut-off for obstruction?
cards.back: FET is 3 s or less. Obstruction is FEV1/FVC <70%.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man who has smoked 45 pack-years has noticed streaks of blood in his morning sputum on most days for six weeks. His voice has become hoarse. His weight is stable.
items.explanation: Repeated small haemoptyses or blood-streaked sputum in a heavy smoker strongly suggest **lung cancer**. Hoarseness points to recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man who moved two months ago from a region where TB is common has a two-month cough with blood in the sputum, soaking night sweats and 6 kg of weight loss.
items.explanation: Haemoptysis with **fever, night sweats and weight loss**, plus a background of high TB exposure, is the classic picture of **tuberculosis**.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman on the combined oral contraceptive pill returned from a long-haul flight three weeks ago. She now has sudden sharp right-sided chest pain on deep breathing, breathlessness and a small amount of bright red blood in her sputum.
items.explanation: Two steps: the pill plus prolonged immobility are risk factors for venous thromboembolism, and **pleuritic pain with dyspnoea and haemoptysis** fits pulmonary infarction. Always consider PE in haemoptysis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman reports episodes of breathlessness during exam week. She says she cannot get a deep enough breath in, sighs frequently, and her fingers and lips tingle. The episodes come at rest and never wake her at night. Examination, chest X-ray and spirometry are normal, and PE has been excluded.
questions.leadIn: Which arterial blood gas pattern is most likely during an episode?
options: Normal PO2, low PCO2, raised pH
Low PO2, low PCO2, raised pH
Low PO2, high PCO2, low pH
Normal PO2, normal PCO2, normal pH
Normal PO2, high PCO2, low pH
questions.explanation: This is **psychogenic hyperventilation**: the patient cannot take a satisfying breath, sighs, has perioral and digital paraesthesiae from alkalosis, and the episodes come at rest without nocturnal waking. Overbreathing washes out CO2, so the gas shows **normal PO2, low PCO2 and alkalosis**. Make the diagnosis only after other causes, especially thromboembolism, are excluded.
whyNot: A low PO2 would suggest a lung or vascular cause such as PE, not anxiety-driven overbreathing.
Hypoxia with hypercapnia and acidosis is type 2 respiratory failure.
During an episode the PCO2 falls, so a completely normal gas is unlikely.
A high PCO2 means hypoventilation, the opposite of what happens here.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with COPD says he can dress and go out alone, but walking on the flat he has to stop for breath after about 100 metres.
questions.leadIn: What is his MRC dyspnoea grade?
questions.explanation: On the MRC scale, **stopping for breath after about 100 m on the level is grade 4**. Grade 5 is being too breathless to leave the house or breathless while dressing. Davidson also advises recording the actual distance walked and stairs climbed.
whyNot: Grade 1 is breathlessness only with strenuous exercise.
Grade 2 is breathlessness on hurrying along the flat or climbing a gentle slope.
Grade 3 is walking slower than peers or stopping at own pace on the level, which is milder than stopping after 100 m.
Grade 5 means being housebound by breathlessness, or breathless while dressing, and he can go out and dress.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman has never worked outside the home. Thirty-five years ago her husband was a shipyard fitter, and she washed his overalls every week. She now has a dull, constant left chest ache, breathlessness and a large left pleural effusion.
items.explanation: Two steps: washing a dockyard worker's clothes is **indirect asbestos exposure**, and even trivial exposure can cause **mesothelioma** decades later (up to about 30 years). Asbestosis needs heavy exposure and causes fibrosis rather than a painful effusion.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man keeps racing pigeons. A few hours after cleaning out the loft he repeatedly gets fever, aching muscles, a dry cough and breathlessness. He has no wheeze.
items.explanation: A flu-like illness **hours after exposure, without wheeze**, is extrinsic allergic alveolitis. Bird droppings and feathers make it **bird fancier's lung**.

items.stem: A 36-year-old factory worker has had cough, chest tightness and wheeze for six months. They are much better at weekends and disappear during a two-week holiday, then return within days of going back to work.
items.explanation: Improvement away from work at weekends and on holiday is the key clue to **occupational asthma**, the commonest occupational lung disease.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old ex-smoker is examined in a respiratory clinic. His fingers show loss of the nail-fold angle and a bulbous tip.
questions.leadIn: Which condition is LEAST likely to explain this sign on its own?
questions.explanation: **COPD does not cause clubbing.** If a COPD patient is clubbed, look for another cause, especially lung cancer. The other four are classic thoracic causes, which make up about 80% of acquired clubbing.
whyNot: Lung cancer is the classic cause of clubbing, sometimes with hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy.
Chronic suppuration (bronchiectasis, abscess, empyema, CF) causes clubbing.
Clubbing is common in IPF.
Mesothelioma is a recognised thoracic tumour cause.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old smoker has had aching pain in his right shoulder and down the inner arm for three months. The small muscles of his right hand are wasted, and his right pupil is smaller than the left with a slightly drooping right eyelid.
questions.leadIn: Where is the underlying lesion most likely to be?
options: Anterior mediastinum compressing the superior vena cava
questions.explanation: Hand muscle wasting (T1 root invasion) with **Horner syndrome** (miosis, ptosis) on the same side is the picture of an **apical (Pancoast) tumour**.
whyNot: A lower lobe tumour does not reach the T1 root or the sympathetic chain.
A left-sided lesion would not cause right-sided Horner syndrome and hand wasting.
SVC obstruction causes facial plethora, swelling and dilated veins, not Horner syndrome with hand wasting.
A central bronchial tumour causes cough, haemoptysis or collapse, not apical nerve signs.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Coarse crackles that change after coughing
Absent breath sounds with absent vocal resonance

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has two years of steadily worsening breathlessness and a dry cough. She is clubbed, and her CT shows basal reticular fibrosis. What do you expect to hear at both bases?
items.explanation: **Fine late or pan-inspiratory "Velcro" crackles** are typical of pulmonary fibrosis/ILD.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has coughed up a cupful of thick green sputum every day since severe whooping cough in childhood. What added sound do you expect over the affected lower zones?
items.explanation: Chronic copious purulent sputum after childhood whooping cough suggests **bronchiectasis**. The retained secretions give **coarse crackles that alter with coughing**.

items.stem: A 63-year-old smoker has haemoptysis. Bronchoscopy shows a tumour partly blocking the right upper lobe bronchus. Over the right upper chest, what do you expect to hear?
items.explanation: A single partly obstructed bronchus produces a **fixed monophonic wheeze** that persists after coughing, a classic sign of bronchial carcinoma. Polyphonic wheeze implies many narrowed small airways.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man has had fever and a productive cough for three days. His trachea is central. Over the left lower zone, expansion is reduced, the note is dull, breath sounds are bronchial and vocal resonance is increased, with crackles.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely lesion?
options: Left lower lobe collapse from central bronchial obstruction
questions.explanation: Dullness with **bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance**, a central trachea and fever describe **consolidation**.
whyNot: An effusion is stony dull with reduced or absent breath sounds and vocal resonance.
Collapse behind a blocked central bronchus reduces breath sounds and vocal resonance and pulls the trachea across.
A pneumothorax is resonant or hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds.
Diffuse fibrosis is bilateral, with fine crackles and no bronchial breathing.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with known asthma is assessed in the emergency department. RR is 28/min, HR 115/min, peak flow 45% of predicted, and she speaks only in short phrases.
questions.leadIn: Which additional finding would move her from severe to life-threatening asthma?
questions.explanation: Life-threatening features include **SpO2 <92%**, PEF <33%, a silent chest, exhaustion, cyanosis and haemodynamic instability. The other options still fall in the severe band.
whyNot: RR >25 already marks severe; a slightly higher rate is not a life-threatening criterion.
HR >110 is a severe feature, not a life-threatening one.
PEF 33–50% is severe; life-threatening needs PEF <33%.
Audible wheeze shows air is still moving. A silent chest is the danger sign.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man is brought in after a car crash. HR 130/min, BP 80/50 mmHg. The trachea is deviated to the left. The right side is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds.
items.explanation: Mediastinal shift away from a hyper-resonant, silent side plus **hypotension and tachycardia** is a **tension pneumothorax**. Decompress immediately without waiting for imaging.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man had TB treated 50 years ago. His trachea is pulled to the right, the right upper chest is flattened, and there is a dull note, bronchial breathing and coarse crackles over the right upper zone.
items.explanation: Two steps: healed TB can leave the damaged lung replaced by scar tissue, and **localised upper lobe fibrosis** pulls the trachea towards it while giving dullness, bronchial breathing and coarse crackles. Collapse also pulls the trachea, but it would not explain the long history or coarse crackles.

items.stem: A 68-year-old smoker has a barrel-shaped chest, a cricosternal distance of one finger-breadth, and costal margins that move inward on inspiration. The apex beat cannot be felt, and cardiac dullness is lost.
items.explanation: Reduced cricosternal distance, **Hoover sign**, an impalpable apex and loss of cardiac dullness are signs of **hyperinflation in COPD**.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with known lung cancer has a trachea deviated to the left. The left upper zone is dull with diminished breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance. There are no chest scars.
items.explanation: Volume loss (trachea pulled towards) with dullness and **reduced** breath sounds means the airway is blocked: **lobar collapse from central obstruction**. With a patent bronchus you would hear bronchial breathing.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman was started on lisinopril for hypertension eight weeks ago. She now has a persistent dry, tickly cough. Examination, chest X-ray and spirometry are normal. She has never smoked.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of her cough?
questions.explanation: The timing after starting an **ACE inhibitor** and the dry, tickly character point to a drug cough, which affects 10–15% of users, more often women.
whyNot: Cough-variant asthma is a common cause of chronic cough with normal tests, but the clear drug timeline makes it less likely.
GORD is possible but would usually come with heartburn or reflux.
Lung cancer is unlikely in a never-smoker with a normal X-ray and an obvious drug trigger.
Post-nasal drip usually comes with rhinitis or sinus symptoms.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has had a slowly worsening harsh noise on breathing in for four months. Her voice is hoarse. The noise is loudest over the neck and is absent on breathing out.
questions.leadIn: Where is the problem located?
options: Large airway outside the thorax (larynx or upper trachea)
questions.explanation: An inspiratory noise loudest over the trachea is **stridor**. It means narrowing of a major **extrathoracic** airway, here a slowly growing laryngeal or tracheal lesion, and needs urgent assessment.
whyNot: Small airway narrowing gives polyphonic, mainly expiratory wheeze.
Pleural inflammation gives a rub and pleuritic pain.
Alveolar fluid produces crackles, not a noise loudest at the neck.
Interstitial disease gives fine late inspiratory crackles.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man who drinks heavily wakes with nausea, retches several times, and then brings up dark red blood mixed with food. He has no cough.
questions.leadIn: What best describes this bleeding?
questions.explanation: Blood that follows **nausea and retching** and is mixed with vomit is **haematemesis**. True haemoptysis is coughed up and mixed with sputum. Always establish the source first.
whyNot: Haemoptysis is coughed up and mixed with sputum, not vomited with food.
Nasopharyngeal blood simply appears in the mouth without vomiting.
Pulmonary infarction causes coughed-up blood with pleuritic pain.
A lung abscess causes cough with foul purulent sputum.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man is referred with wheeze that began a year after he started a new factory job.
questions.leadIn: Which history feature most strongly supports occupational asthma?
options: Symptoms improve at weekends and on holiday
Symptoms first appeared 30 years after exposure
Fever and muscle aches a few hours after exposure, without wheeze
Cough that is worse when lying flat
questions.explanation: Improvement **away from work** is the key clue to occupational asthma, the commonest occupational lung disease.
whyNot: Long latency is typical of asbestos-related disease such as mesothelioma.
This describes extrinsic allergic alveolitis, which does not cause wheeze.
Cough on lying flat suggests pulmonary oedema (or reflux).
This is non-specific and does not link symptoms to work.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man has had COPD for ten years. At review his fingers are newly clubbed, and he mentions two episodes of blood-streaked sputum in the past month.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation for the clubbing?
questions.explanation: Step 1: COPD itself **does not cause clubbing** and rarely causes haemoptysis. Step 2: new clubbing in a long-term smoker therefore needs another explanation. Step 3: repeated small haemoptyses also point to cancer. Together, these make **bronchial carcinoma** the likely cause. Smoker + haemoptysis + clubbing is a classic exam triad.
whyNot: COPD, however severe, does not cause clubbing.
Inhaled steroids do not cause clubbing (long-term oral steroids cause thin skin and bruising).
CO2 retention gives warm hands, a bounding pulse and a flap, not clubbing.
Cor pulmonale gives raised JVP and oedema, not clubbing.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with severe COPD now sleeps on three pillows because he becomes more breathless lying flat. He has no history of angina, myocardial infarction or hypertension, and his heart sounds are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the best interpretation of his orthopnoea?
options: It can arise from COPD itself and does not establish heart failure
questions.explanation: Step 1: orthopnoea is often taught as a cardiac symptom. Step 2: Davidson points out that lying flat lets the abdominal contents push the diaphragm up, which **worsens airflow obstruction**, so orthopnoea is common in COPD. Step 3: it only points to the heart when there is a history suggesting cardiac disease, and here there is none. So it **does not establish heart failure**.
whyNot: Orthopnoea is not specific to LVF. Without a cardiac history it does not confirm it.
A pneumothorax causes sudden pain and breathlessness, not a chronic posture-related pattern.
Psychogenic breathlessness occurs at rest and rarely affects sleep.
Acute asthma presents with episodic wheeze and nocturnal waking, not years of posture-related breathlessness in COPD.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with known left-sided bronchiectasis coughs up about 300 mL of fresh blood over two hours. She is pale and tachycardic but alert.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Lie her on her left side, give high-flow oxygen and resuscitate
Lie her on her right side and give oxygen
Lie her flat on her back and give oxygen
Perform urgent flexible bronchoscopy before resuscitation
questions.explanation: Step 1: over 200–250 mL in 24 h is **massive haemoptysis**, an emergency. Step 2: nurse her upright or **on the bleeding side** (left), so blood does not spill into the good lung. Step 3: give **high-flow oxygen and resuscitate**. Tranexamic acid or terlipressin may help, and bronchial artery embolisation or surgery can save life. Early bronchoscopy often just shows blood throughout the airways.
whyNot: Lying on the good (right) side lets blood run into the healthy lung.
Lying flat does not protect the good lung and may worsen gas exchange.
Bronchoscopy during brisk bleeding is difficult and must not delay resuscitation.
This is an emergency, so outpatient investigation is inappropriate.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A tall, thin 19-year-old man who smokes is watching television when he gets sudden sharp left-sided chest pain and breathlessness.
items.explanation: Instant onset of pleuritic pain and dyspnoea in a **tall, thin young smoker** is the classic **primary spontaneous pneumothorax**.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has 18 months of relentlessly worsening breathlessness, now even at rest, with a dry cough. He is clubbed and has bibasal fine late inspiratory crackles.
items.explanation: Steadily progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, clubbing and **Velcro crackles** indicate **interstitial lung disease** (fibrosis).

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy choked while eating peanuts an hour ago. He now coughs repeatedly, and wheeze is heard over the right side only.
items.explanation: Two steps: a sudden choking episode while eating, then **unilateral wheeze** (a focal lesion rather than asthma) means an **inhaled foreign body**, which is commonest in children.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman is stung by a wasp. Within minutes she has facial swelling, inspiratory stridor, wheeze and a BP of 75/40 mmHg.
items.explanation: Onset within minutes of an allergen with **stridor, angio-oedema and hypotension** is **anaphylaxis**.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man has been taking an antiarrhythmic for recurrent atrial fibrillation for three years. He has six months of progressive breathlessness and bibasal fine crackles.
items.explanation: Of the drugs that cause ILD, **amiodarone** is the one used to control AF.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with mild, previously quiet asthma becomes wheezy two weeks after his ophthalmologist starts treatment for glaucoma.
items.explanation: Topical beta-blockers such as **timolol eye drops** are absorbed enough to cause bronchospasm. This is why you ask specifically about non-oral drugs.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with asthma and nasal polyps develops severe wheeze about an hour after taking a painkiller for back pain.
items.explanation: Wheeze shortly after aspirin or an **NSAID** in an asthmatic, often with nasal polyps, is aspirin/NSAID-sensitive asthma.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman has been treated for polymyalgia rheumatica for two years. She now has night sweats, weight loss and a cavitating shadow in the right upper lobe.
items.explanation: Two steps: the illness is likely **tuberculosis**, and **long-term oral steroids** (her polymyalgia treatment) predispose to TB and pneumocystis.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman taking adjuvant hormonal therapy after breast cancer has sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness, and her calf is swollen.
items.explanation: Tamoxifen (like oestrogens and raloxifene) raises the risk of **venous thromboembolism**, here PE.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has an Hb of 60 g/L. She is admitted with pneumonia, and her SpO2 is 84% on air, but her tongue and lips look pink.
questions.leadIn: What best explains the absence of central cyanosis?
options: Cyanosis needs a fixed amount of deoxygenated Hb, which is harder to reach when Hb is low
Pulse oximetry overestimates hypoxia whenever Hb is low
Central cyanosis is best seen in the fingers rather than the tongue
Central cyanosis occurs only in congenital heart disease
Pneumonia causes peripheral but never central cyanosis
questions.explanation: Central cyanosis appears at about **50 g/L of deoxygenated Hb**. With severe anaemia there is too little Hb to reach that level, so cyanosis appears late or not at all. Its **absence never excludes hypoxia**.
whyNot: The issue is how cyanosis is produced, not oximeter error.
Central cyanosis is best seen on the tongue and lips. Blue fingers alone may be peripheral.
Central cyanosis occurs in any cause of significant arterial desaturation, including lung disease.
Pneumonia causing significant hypoxaemia can produce central cyanosis.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man was found unconscious after an alcohol binge two weeks ago. He now has a swinging fever and coughs up dark, foul-tasting sputum.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Alcohol binges with reduced consciousness lead to **aspiration**. **Foul-smelling, dark sputum** suggests a **lung abscess** with anaerobes.
whyNot: Bronchiectasis gives long-standing daily purulent sputum, not a two-week illness after aspiration.
Pulmonary oedema produces pink frothy secretions.
Asthma causes wheeze and dry cough or mucoid sputum.
Infarction causes pleuritic pain and haemoptysis, not foul sputum.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Wasting of the small hand muscles
Plethoric facial swelling with dilated chest-wall veins

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with COPD is drowsy and confused on arrival. His hands are warm and his pulse is bounding. Which further sign of the same problem should you look for?
items.explanation: Two steps: drowsiness with warm hands and a bounding pulse in COPD suggests **CO2 retention**. Its signs are warm peripheries, a bounding pulse, confusion and a **coarse flap**, which is a late and non-specific sign.

items.stem: A 58-year-old smoker with lung cancer has increasing breathlessness. Raising both arms above his head makes his face congested and blue. What is the most likely visible sign?
items.explanation: A positive **Pemberton sign** (facial congestion and cyanosis when the arms are raised) points to **SVC obstruction**, usually from lung cancer compressing the vein. Expect facial plethora and swelling with dilated neck and chest veins.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has recurrent pleural effusions, bronchiectasis and swollen legs from lymphoedema. What nail finding is expected?
items.explanation: Effusions, bronchiectasis and lymphoedema together make up **yellow nail syndrome**: thick yellow nails, often with onycholysis.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman has progressive breathlessness. Spirometry shows reduced FEV1 and reduced FVC, with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 90%. Her forced expiratory time is 2 s.
questions.leadIn: Which pattern is shown?
options: Restrictive defect, as in interstitial lung disease
Mixed obstructive defect with poor effort
questions.explanation: Both volumes are reduced with a **normal or high ratio**, which is restriction (ILD, sarcoidosis, chest wall disease). Obstruction would give FEV1/FVC <70% and a prolonged forced expiratory time.
whyNot: Asthma is obstructive: the ratio is below 70%.
COPD is obstructive with a low ratio and a prolonged FET.
FEV1 and FVC are both reduced, so this is not normal.
A high ratio with a short FET rules out obstruction.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has had fever and a productive cough for two days. You want the single examination finding that most increases the likelihood of pneumonia.
questions.leadIn: Which finding has the highest positive likelihood ratio?
questions.explanation: In Talley's evidence summary, **aegophony** has the highest LR+ for pneumonia (about 5.3), followed by dullness (4.3), bronchial breathing and crackles (3.5 each), and fever (2.4).
whyNot: Dullness is useful (LR+ about 4.3) but less than aegophony.
Bronchial breathing has LR+ about 3.5.
Crackles have LR+ about 3.5.
Fever over 37.8 °C has the lowest LR+ of these (about 2.4).

questions.stem: A 54-year-old smoker has his trachea deviated to the right. The right upper zone is dull, with reduced expansion and reduced breath sounds. His chest X-ray shows a raised horizontal fissure and a right hilar mass.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Trachea pulled **towards** a dull upper zone with a **raised horizontal fissure** means loss of right upper lobe volume, i.e. **collapse**. Here it is probably caused by a central tumour (hilar mass) blocking the bronchus, hence the reduced breath sounds.
whyNot: Consolidation does not move the trachea and gives bronchial breathing.
An effusion is stony dull at the base and pushes the trachea away only if massive.
A left tension pneumothorax would push the trachea right, but the right upper zone would not be dull and the patient would be shocked.
A pneumothorax is resonant, not dull.

ospe.identify: Finger clubbing: loss of the nail-fold (hyponychial) angle and a bulbous fingertip. Think lung cancer, suppurative lung disease or fibrosis, never COPD alone.
Clinical clubbing. Name the sign and give three thoracic causes (bronchial carcinoma, bronchiectasis, pulmonary fibrosis).
Yellow nail syndrome: thick yellow nails with onycholysis. It goes with pleural effusions, bronchiectasis and lymphoedema.
Barrel chest: increased AP diameter from hyperinflation (emphysema or severe asthma). It can be normal in old age.
Chest wall deformity: pectus excavatum (funnel chest) compared with pectus carinatum (pigeon chest).
Hoover sign: the costal margins move inward on inspiration in a hyperinflated COPD chest (LR+ about 4.2).
Spirometry traces. Obstructive: FEV1/FVC well below 70% (asthma, COPD). Restrictive: small volumes with a normal or high ratio (ILD).
Left upper lobe collapse on CXR: hazy left upper and mid zones with volume loss, and the trachea and heart pulled to the left.
